summary: Discusses how to protect block storage protocols running over IP using IPsec and IKE. It develops threat models and security approaches for iSCSI, iFCP and FCIP, plus the iSNS and SLPv2 discovery protocols, and looks at performance and resource limits. It was updated by RFC 7146.

plainLanguage.summary: Sending disk data across a network is risky if others can peek. This explains how to wrap that traffic in a protective tunnel so storage stays private and safe.

subtitle: How to protect iSCSI, iFCP, FCIP and their discovery protocols with IPsec and IKE.

tldr.problem: Block storage protocols such as iSCSI, iFCP and FCIP carry disk commands and data over IP, but SCSI and Fibre Channel rely on physical and administrative security that an IP network cannot assume.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC requires the storage protocols to use IPsec ESP for per-packet authentication, integrity, replay protection and optional confidentiality, with IKE for keying, and it sets the algorithms, modes and interoperability rules for doing so.
tldr.outcome: The security requirements are also built into the iSCSI, iFCP and FCIP standards; this RFC reproduces them and adds analysis. It was later updated by RFC 7146.

sections.title: Three Storage Protocols and IPsec
sections.content:
This RFC covers the use of the IPsec protocol suite to protect block storage protocols over IP: iSCSI, iFCP and FCIP, plus the discovery protocols iSNS and SLPv2.

iSCSI is a connection-oriented command/response protocol that runs over TCP and is used to access disk, tape and other devices. Clients are called initiators and servers are called targets. iFCP is a gateway-to-gateway protocol that provides transport services to Fibre Channel devices over TCP/IP. FCIP is a pure Fibre Channel encapsulation protocol that transports FC frames, aimed at interconnecting Fibre Channel switches.

None of the three has its own in-band per-packet security. iSCSI login can authenticate the endpoints, but the protocols rely on IPsec for confidentiality, integrity and authentication, with IKE as the key management protocol. All three use TCP for congestion control, error detection and error recovery.

The requirements here apply only to IPsec and IKE as used with IP block storage. They are also incorporated into the iSCSI (RFC 3720), iFCP and FCIP documents, and if there is a discrepancy those documents take precedence.
sections.plainLanguage: Computers can talk to far-away disks over a network. The talking has no built-in lock, so this document says to borrow a lock called IPsec.

sections.title: Threats and Security Requirements
sections.content:
Both control and data packets of IP block storage protocols are exposed. The RFC lists attacks such as snooping on data, modifying or injecting packets, hijacking the TCP connections, denial of service (for example by sending a TCP reset), disrupting the security negotiation, impersonating a storage entity, and attacking the discovery process. Because iFCP and FCIP devices guard a whole Fibre Channel island, a successful attack could compromise every host behind them.

The security protocols must therefore support confidentiality, data origin authentication, integrity and replay protection on a per-packet basis, and perfect forward secrecy when rekeying. Bi-directional authentication of the endpoints MUST be provided. The identities used in authentication do not need to be kept confidential.

The mechanism must be feasible at 1 Gbps with the CPU and hardware available, with 10 Gbps highly desirable. Security is mandatory to implement but not mandatory to use: which services apply depends on configuration and policy.

SCSI and Fibre Channel contain little security of their own and depend on physical security, administrative security and correct configuration. For most IP networks that assumption is inappropriate, so authentication SHOULD be used.

For resource limits, the RFC treats code size as the main concern for embedded host bus adapters: 8-10 MB for authentication and keying is clearly excessive, 800-1000 KB is tolerable only if nothing else is possible, and 80-100 KB should be acceptable. These are rough order-of-magnitude guides.
sections.plainLanguage: Disks on a network could be spied on or tricked by bad guys. The rules say every message must be checked, kept fresh and sent only between friends who proved who they are.

sections.title: Required IPsec and IKE Features
sections.content:
Conformant implementations MUST support IPsec ESP for both control and data packets, with per-packet data origin authentication, integrity and replay protection. For confidentiality, ESP with 3DES in CBC mode MUST be supported and AES in Counter mode SHOULD be. For authentication and integrity, HMAC-SHA1 MUST be supported and AES in CBC MAC mode with XCBC extensions SHOULD be. DES in CBC mode SHOULD NOT be used because of its inherent weakness, and ESP with NULL encryption MUST be supported for authentication-only use.

ESP in tunnel mode MUST be supported; transport mode MAY be. IKE MUST be supported for peer authentication, security association negotiation and key management. Manual keying MUST NOT be used because it lacks rekeying support. Peer authentication with a pre-shared key MUST be supported, and certificates with digital signatures MAY be. IKE Main Mode MUST be supported and Aggressive Mode SHOULD be.

Main Mode with a pre-shared key SHOULD NOT be used when either peer has a dynamically assigned address, because that forces a group pre-shared key, which is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attack. Receiving an IKE Phase 2 delete message MUST NOT be taken as a reason to tear down a storage connection.

For interoperability the RFC suggests offering 3DES-CBC with HMAC-SHA1, using a Diffie-Hellman group of at least 1024 bits with that pair and at least 2048 bits if AES-CTR with XCBC-MAC is preferred.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone must know the same few locks and secret handshakes so any two devices can agree on one. Old, weak locks are not allowed, and keys must be changed on a schedule, never set once by hand.

sections.title: iSCSI Login Authentication
sections.content:
iSCSI has its own login-time authentication, but the RFC says it is a weak solution on its own: it can mutually authenticate initiator and target when a connection starts, yet gives no per-packet authentication, integrity, confidentiality or replay protection, and no protected cipher suite negotiation.

Compliant iSCSI implementations MUST implement CHAP with bi-directional authentication. Over an unencrypted channel CHAP is open to off-line dictionary attack, so implementations MUST support random secrets of up to 128 bits and MUST NOT offer any secret generation other than random. If a secret is smaller than 96 bits, IPsec encryption MUST be in use and the login MUST NOT continue unless that can be verified.

The same secret SHOULD NOT be configured for several initiators or targets, since any of them could then impersonate another. A secret for one direction must not be used for the other, and an originator MUST NOT reuse the responder's challenge for the reverse direction; the RFC describes a reflection attack between two connections that these rules block.

Implementations MAY also implement SRP. They MUST use one of the well-known groups in Appendix A, they MUST support the groups up to 1536 bits, and targets MUST always offer SRP-1536.
sections.plainLanguage: When you start talking, both sides prove who they are with a secret password game. The password must be hard to guess, and you may not use the same password for everyone or let a sneaky helper repeat your answer back.

sections.title: Securing Discovery with SLPv2 and iSNS
sections.content:
Devices find each other with SLPv2 (used by iSCSI and FCIP) or iSNS (required for iFCP, optional for iSCSI, not used by FCIP). These can also hand out IPsec policy, such as whether a peer needs IPsec or cleartext, supports perfect forward secrecy, prefers tunnel mode, and allows Main or Aggressive Mode. Learning this first avoids long IKE timeouts. If policy is distributed this way, the discovery protocol is a weak link, so per-packet authentication, integrity and replay protection MUST be used on it.

The RFC finds that SLPv2's own security does not meet the needs: it provides authentication but no confidentiality, and it cannot authenticate zero-result responses, which allows a denial of service attack. It proposes IPsec ESP with a non-null transform on unicast SLPv2 messages instead. Multicast requests stay unprotected, so a user agent MUST check that a reply matches a request it actually sent. An entity that already has its security settings by other means MUST NOT request them via SLPv2 or iSNS.

For iSNS, ESP in tunnel mode MUST be implemented, replay protection MUST be supported, and when iSNS distributes security policy IPsec authentication, integrity and confidentiality MUST protect all its messages. Each registered iSNS client keeps at least one Phase 1 and one Phase 2 security association with the server.
sections.plainLanguage: Before talking, devices look each other up in a phone book. The phone book must not be forgeable either, or you could be sent to a fake friend.

sections.title: How Sessions Map onto IPsec
sections.content:
An iSCSI session may use several TCP connections, and each TCP connection is protected by exactly one IKE Phase 2 security association, though one Phase 2 SA may protect many connections. IPsec and IKE negotiations finish before the initiator contacts the target on well-known TCP port 3260, so a policy such as ESP with a non-null transform for all traffic to that port handles it automatically.

On teardown, iSCSI uses its Logout command for a graceful close. A Phase 2 delete message, which hardware may send to keep the number of active SAs low, MUST NOT be read as a reason to tear down the iSCSI connection; it is preferable to leave it up and bring up a new SA if more traffic is sent.

iFCP and FCIP are peer-to-peer, so bi-directional authentication of gateways MUST be provided. An iFCP Portal has 0..M Phase 1 SAs to a peer, each with 0..N Phase 2 SAs, each protecting 0..Z TCP connections, and unbound connections MUST also be protected. In FCIP each TCP connection in an FCIP Link corresponds to a Phase 2 SA established before the initial TCP SYN is sent.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of one secure tunnel that many conversations can ride through. Closing the tunnel door does not mean the conversation inside has ended.

sections.title: Tunnel Mode, Transport Mode and NAT
sections.content:
The RFC compares IPsec tunnel and transport mode for storage traffic. Tunnel mode adds an extra IP header, which lowers the path MTU and may reduce the TCP maximum segment size. It needs inner and outer addresses configured or discovered, but it lets a firewall terminate the tunnel and verify each packet while the endpoints still communicate end to end. Transport mode keeps IPsec and the application on the same host, allowing tight integration between them.

Tunnel mode ESP can cross a NAT only in limited cases. TCP over transport mode ESP cannot, because the TCP checksum includes a pseudo-header with IP fields and is protected by the ESP integrity check, so a NAT invalidates it. Since TCP checksum verification is mandatory, implementations can instead use IPsec and IKE NAT traversal, which negotiates UDP encapsulation when a NAT is detected.

The RFC also covers IKE fragmentation when certificates are large, which many NATs and firewalls handle badly, and notes that path MTU discovery can fail where IPsec drops unauthenticated ICMP messages.
sections.plainLanguage: You can wrap each package in a new outer box, or lock the original box. The outer box is easier for guards to check but makes the parcel bigger. A mail sorter who rewrites the address on a locked box makes the lock look broken.

sections.title: Rekeying, Speed and the iSCSI CRC
sections.content:
At storage speeds a single IPsec SA can burn through its 32-bit sequence number space quickly. The RFC calculates that at 1 Gbps with 64 octet packets this takes 2200 seconds (37 minutes), and at 10 Gbps 220 seconds (3.67 minutes). With CBC ciphers an SA must also be rekeyed before 2^(n/2) blocks are sent, where n is the block size in bits. For 3DES, with a 64-bit block, that means rekeying about every 274.9 seconds at 1 Gbps and every 27.5 seconds at 10 Gbps. This limit does not apply to counter mode.

iSCSI adds a 32-bit CRC to its headers and data because the 16-bit TCP checksum may miss errors at high speed. IPsec authentication transforms give stronger integrity protection, so where IPsec integrity is in place end to end, CRC failure recovery can be simplified or the CRC omitted, for example when IPsec, TCP and CRC checks are all offloaded to the NIC. It remains useful in pure software stacks, in iSCSI proxies and where IPsec is provided by an external device.

Appendix B reports software performance measurements of IPsec transforms, which this explainer does not summarize.
sections.plainLanguage: A fast network uses up its numbered tickets quickly, so the lock needs new keys and new tickets often. The extra check number iSCSI already adds can sometimes be skipped when the lock already does the checking.
